questions.q: A square of side 7 cm is inscribed in a circle. What is the area of the circle not covered by the square?
questions.a: Diagonal of square = diameter of circle. Diagonal = 7√2 cm, so radius = 7√2/2 = 7/√2 cm. Area of circle = π(7/√2)² = π × 49/2 = 49π/2 cm². Area of square = 49 cm². Shaded area = 49π/2 − 49 = 49(π/2 − 1) ≈ 49(0.57) ≈ 27.97 cm². A wrong answer (e.g., using side as radius) shows the student does not know that the diagonal of an inscribed square equals the diameter.

questions.q: A rectangle 20 cm × 14 cm has a semicircle on its shorter side. Find the total area.
questions.a: Area of rectangle = 20 × 14 = 280 cm². The semicircle is on the shorter side (14 cm), so its diameter = 14 cm, radius = 7 cm. Area of semicircle = (1/2)π(7)² = 49π/2 ≈ 77 cm². Total area = 280 + 49π/2 ≈ 357 cm². A wrong answer (e.g., using full circle area instead of semicircle) shows the student did not identify the shape correctly.

questions.q: A sector of a circle of radius 6 cm with central angle 60° contains an equilateral triangle. Find the area of the shaded region (sector minus triangle).
questions.a: Area of sector = (60/360) × π × 36 = 6π cm². The triangle inscribed in a 60° sector with two radii as sides is equilateral with side 6 cm. Area = (√3/4) × 36 = 9√3 cm². Shaded area = 6π − 9√3 ≈ 18.85 − 15.59 = 3.26 cm². A wrong answer (e.g., not recognising the triangle is equilateral) shows the student cannot identify the inscribed polygon.

questions.q: A circle is inscribed in a square of side 14 cm. Find the area between the square and the circle.
questions.a: Side of square = diameter of inscribed circle = 14 cm, so radius = 7 cm. Area of square = 196 cm². Area of circle = π × 49 = 49π ≈ 154 cm². Area between = 196 − 49π ≈ 196 − 154 = 42 cm². A wrong answer (e.g., using 14 as radius) confuses the inscribed and circumscribed cases.

questions.q: Why do we subtract areas in some composite figures and add in others?
questions.a: We ADD when the component shapes do not overlap (adjacent regions, like a rectangle with a semicircle on top). We SUBTRACT when one shape is inside another (inscribed figures, like a square in a circle) and we want the area of the outer shape not covered by the inner. The decision depends on whether the shaded region is a UNION (add) or a DIFFERENCE (subtract) of the component areas. A wrong answer (e.g., "always add") shows the student does not understand the geometric relationship between the shapes.

questions.q: A running track consists of a rectangle 100 m × 60 m with semicircles on both shorter sides. Find the total area of the track.
questions.a: The two semicircles (on the 60 m sides) together form a full circle of diameter 60 m, radius 30 m. Area of rectangle = 100 × 60 = 6000 m². Area of circle = π × 900 = 900π m². Total area = 6000 + 900π ≈ 6000 + 2827 = 8827 m². A wrong answer (e.g., adding two separate semicircle areas without combining) shows the student does not recognise that two semicircles on opposite sides make a full circle.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The area of a ______ of plane figures (such as a circle and a polygon) is found by adding or subtracting the areas of the individual component shapes.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a ______ park with a square fountain built inside it.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can decompose a composite figure involving circles and polygons into its component shapes, identify which areas to add and which to subtract, compute each area using the appropriate formula, and combine them to find the total or shaded area.
